title: Space Complexity and the Call Stack
summary: What counts as extra memory, why every recursive call is a stack frame that costs real space, and why 'no extra variables' doesn't mean O(1) space once recursion is involved.

slides.markdown:
Every complexity discussion so far in this group has been about time. **Space complexity** asks a parallel question: how much extra memory does an algorithm use, as a function of input size n?

The rule that surprises the most candidates: **recursion isn't free memory-wise, even when the function has no arrays, lists, or extra variables.** Every unreturned recursive call is a live stack frame sitting in memory, and a function that recurses to depth n uses O(n) space on the call stack alone — no different, in Big-O terms, from allocating an explicit array of size n.

This is why an interviewer who asks "what's the space complexity" after you write a recursive solution is checking something specific: do you count the stack, or only the variables you can see on the page.

slides.subTitle: Why the input itself usually isn't counted
slides.markdown:
**Total space** is everything the algorithm touches, including the input itself. **Auxiliary space** is everything *beyond* the input — the extra memory the algorithm itself allocates. By convention, when someone says "the space complexity is O(n)" in an interview, they mean **auxiliary space** unless stated otherwise, because the input has to be stored somewhere regardless of which algorithm you pick.

Concretely: an in-place array reversal takes the n-element input as given and uses O(1) *auxiliary* space (a couple of swap variables), even though the *total* space (input + auxiliary) is O(n). Sorting a copy of the array into a new list is O(n) *auxiliary*, because now the algorithm itself owns an extra n-sized allocation on top of the input.

Saying "O(1) space" without the auxiliary qualifier is ambiguous — the strong answer names which one you mean, especially when comparing an in-place approach to one that isn't.

slides.sectionTitle: The call stack is memory too
slides.markdown:
Every function call — recursive or not — pushes a **stack frame** onto the call stack: the function's local variables, its parameters, and the address to return to once it finishes. That frame stays allocated until the call returns.

For an ordinary loop, at most one frame (the enclosing function's) exists at a time — O(1) stack space regardless of how many iterations run. For a **recursive** function, every call that hasn't returned yet has a live frame still on the stack, and those frames stack up while the recursion goes deeper.

So the relevant quantity for recursive space is not how many total calls happen (that's a time question), but **how deep the recursion goes at its deepest point** — the maximum number of simultaneously-live frames. That's a genuinely different number from the total call count, and conflating them is the single most common space-complexity mistake with recursive code.

For a function that recurses linearly to depth n — like a naive recursive sum over a list — the stack grows one frame per call and only starts shrinking once the base case returns and calls start unwinding. At the deepest point, there are **n frames alive simultaneously**, each holding that call's local state. That's O(n) space, even if each individual frame holds nothing but a single integer.

Contrast this with the recursion tree from `recursion-recurrences-and-the-recursion-tree`: that diagram showed *all* calls, including ones that had already returned, to reason about *total time*. The stack diagram only ever shows the calls **currently active on one root-to-leaf path** — a much smaller picture, and the right one for space.

slides.sectionTitle: Iterative O(1) space vs recursive O(n) space
slides.markdown:
| Version | Time | Space | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Iterative sum with a loop | O(n) | O(1) | one frame, one accumulator variable, reused every iteration |
| Recursive sum, `return arr[0] + sum(arr[1:])` | O(n) | O(n) | n live stack frames at maximum depth, one per unreturned call |

Same time complexity, same logical result, genuinely different space complexity. The recursive version isn't "a loop written differently" from a space standpoint — it's closer to allocating an explicit array of size n, except the allocation is implicit and easy to overlook because there's no visible `new Array(n)` anywhere in the code.

This is exactly why a recursive solution that's asymptotically fine on time can still fail in production with a **stack overflow** on a large input, while an equivalent loop never would — the failure mode is specific to how the language implements function calls, not to the algorithm's logic being wrong.

slides.sectionTitle: "No extra variables, so it's O(1) space"
slides.subTitle: The stack disagrees
slides.markdown:
A candidate writes a recursive function with no arrays, no extra lists, seemingly no memory allocation at all — and calls it O(1) space because they can't point to any variable that grows. This misses the frames entirely.

```python
def sum_list(arr, i=0):
    if i == len(arr):
        return 0
    return arr[i] + sum_list(arr, i + 1)   # no visible "extra" data structure
```

There's no list, no dict, nothing that looks like it's holding n things — and yet this is **O(n) space**, because each of the n recursive calls before the base case adds a stack frame, and all n are alive simultaneously at maximum depth. The memory is real; it's just implicit, managed by the runtime rather than written by hand.

The fix for the reasoning: space complexity of recursive code always has to account for **maximum simultaneous call depth**, not just the variables visibly declared inside the function body.

slides.sectionTitle: Tail recursion in theory vs practice
slides.subTitle: Why Python, JS, and Java don't optimize it away
slides.markdown:
A recursive call is in **tail position** if it's the very last operation the function performs — nothing happens after it returns except passing its result straight up. In theory, a compiler can recognize this and reuse the current stack frame instead of pushing a new one, since there's nothing left in the current frame worth keeping around. This is called **tail-call optimization (TCO)**, and where it's implemented, tail-recursive code runs in O(1) stack space regardless of depth.

The catch: **Python, JavaScript (in most engines), and standard Java do not implement TCO.** A tail-recursive function in these languages still pushes a full frame per call and can still stack-overflow at depth ~1,000–10,000 depending on the runtime, even though the same code in a language that does optimize it (Scheme, and some functional languages) would run in constant space.

The practical consequence: "just make it tail-recursive" is not a reliable space-complexity fix in the languages most interviews are conducted in. Converting to an explicit loop is the actual fix — covered next.

slides.sectionTitle: Rewriting linear recursion as a loop
Where this compounds with time complexity
slides.markdown:
Space and time complexity are analyzed separately, but a recursive algorithm's space cost is always bounded by its **deepest single path**, not its total call count — which is why an exponential-time recursion can still have modest space usage.

Naive Fibonacci (`recursion-recurrences-and-the-recursion-tree`) makes O(2ⁿ) total calls — but at any instant, only one root-to-leaf path is ever live on the stack, so its space complexity is a comparatively mild **O(n)**, not O(2ⁿ). This is a useful sanity check: **time complexity comes from the whole tree; space complexity comes from the tree's height, never its total node count.**

The practical read for an interview: always report time and space as two separate numbers, and derive space from "how deep can this recursion go before the first return," not from anything you computed for the time analysis.

A complete space answer names: **whether you mean auxiliary or total** ("O(1) auxiliary, not counting the input"), **whether the call stack counts** ("O(n) on the call stack, since this recurses to depth n"), and, if relevant, **whether an iterative rewrite would help** ("I could convert this to a loop to drop stack space to O(1), at the cost of managing the state explicitly").

That last point is a real design decision, not just a factoid — some algorithms are dramatically clearer written recursively, and trading a little stack space for readability is a defensible choice as long as you know you're making it. The next topic makes that trade-off explicit and general: deliberately spending memory — via memoization, precomputed tables, or hashing — to buy speed, as an intentional interview-optimization lever rather than a side effect of how you happened to write the code.
